class _Line:
    """A line in repr output."""

    parent: Optional["_Line"] = None
    is_root: bool = False
    node: Optional[Node] = None
    text: str = ""
    suffix: str = ""
    whitespace: str = ""
    expanded: bool = False

    @property

        """Check if the line may be expanded."""
        return bool(self.node is not None and self.node.children)

    def check_length(self, max_length: int) -> bool:
        """Check this line fits within a given number of cells."""
        start_length = (
            len(self.whitespace) + cell_len(self.text) + cell_len(self.suffix)

        return self.node.check_length(start_length, max_length)

    def expand(self, indent_size: int) -> Iterable["_Line"]:
        """Expand this line by adding children on their own line."""
        node = self.node
        assert node is not None
        whitespace = self.whitespace
        assert node.children
        if node.key_repr:
            new_line = yield _Line(
                text=f"{node.key_repr}{node.key_separator}{node.open_brace}",
                whitespace=whitespace,
            )
        else:
            new_line = yield _Line(text=node.open_brace, whitespace=whitespace)
        child_whitespace = self.whitespace + " " * indent_size
        tuple_of_one = node.is_tuple and len(node.children) == 1
        for last, child in loop_last(node.children):
            separator = "," if tuple_of_one else node.separator
            line = _Line(
                parent=new_line,
                node=child,
                whitespace=child_whitespace,
                suffix=separator,
                last=last and not tuple_of_one,
            )
            yield line

        yield _Line(
            text=node.close_brace,
            whitespace=whitespace,
            suffix=self.suffix,
            last=self.last,
        )

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        if self.last:
            return f"{self.whitespace}{self.text}{self.node or ''}"
        else:
            return (

def _is_namedtuple(obj: Any) -> bool:
    """Checks if an object is most likely a namedtuple. It is possible
    to craft an object that passes this check and isn't a namedtuple, but
    there is only a minuscule chance of this happening unintentionally.

    Args:
        obj (Any): The object to test

    Returns:
        bool: True if the object is a namedtuple. False otherwise.
    """
    try:
        fields = getattr(obj, "_fields", None)
    except Exception:
        # Being very defensive - if we cannot get the attr then its not a namedtuple
        return False
    return isinstance(obj, tuple) and isinstance(fields, tuple)

steps.message:
Aha!

```python
        style._hash = self._hash
```

In `clear_meta_and_links`, the new `style` object is given the SAME `_hash` as the original `style` object.

But the new `style` object has `_link = None` and `_meta = None`.
The original `style` object might have had a `_link` or `_meta`.

If the original `style` had `_meta` or `_link`, its hash was computed including those.
The new `style` object should have a DIFFERENT hash because its `_link` and `_meta` are now `None`.

By doing `style._hash = self._hash`, the new `style` object is incorrectly given the hash of the original `style` object.

This is exactly what "the hashed cache is not being cleared when 'meta' is cleared" means! (And also when link is cleared).

To fix this, `style._hash` should be set to `None` in `clear_meta_and_links`, so that it is recomputed when needed.

Let's verify this.

If I have a `Style` with `meta={"foo": "bar"}`, its hash is `H1`.
If I call `clear_meta_and_links()`, I get a new `Style` with `meta=None`.
But this new `Style` also has `_hash = H1`.
If I then compare this new `Style` with another `Style` that has `meta=None` and same other attributes, its hash will be `H2`.
So `Style(meta={"foo": "bar"}).clear_meta_and_links() == Style(meta=None)` will be `False` because `H1 != H2`.

Wait, `__eq__` uses `__hash__`.

```python
    def __eq__(self, other: Any) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Style):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.__hash__() == other.__hash__()
```

And `__hash__` returns `self._hash` if it's not `None`.

```python
    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        if self._hash is not None:
            return self._hash
        # ...
```

So yes, if `style._hash = self._hash` is used in `clear_meta_and_links`, the new style will have the wrong hash.

The fix is to set `style._hash = None`.

Summary:
The bug was in `rich/style.py` in the `clear_meta_and_links` method. It was incorrectly copying the hash of the original `Style` object to the new one, even though the new one had different properties (no meta or links). This caused equality comparisons to fail. I changed `style._hash = self._hash` to `style._hash = None`, which forces the hash to be recomputed correctly.

The bug was located in `rich/style.py` within the `clear_meta_and_links` method. When creating a new `Style` object without meta and link information, the method was incorrectly copying the hash of the original object (`style._hash = self._hash`). Since the hash of a `Style` object depends on its meta and link attributes, the new object ended up with an incorrect hash, causing it to fail equality comparisons with other `Style` objects that were correctly initialized without meta/link data.

I fixed this by changing the assignment to `style._hash = None`, which ensures that the hash is recomputed correctly upon the first request. I verified the fix using a reproduction script that confirmed the corrected behavior.
